target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would reduce scheduling barriers and therefore increase voting access for millions.
objection: A federal holiday does not force private employers to close or provide paid leave, so many retail and service workers—especially low-income hourly workers—would still have to work on Election Day and would not see their voting barrier removed.

target: AG1's assumption that a national holiday would not worsen equity and could help low-income voters broadly.
objection: If holiday flexibility helps some groups while leaving low-income workers' work-time barriers intact, then the policy could fail to improve, or even widen, inequities in voting access rather than reduce them.

target: AG1's idea that making Election Day a national holiday is an effective turnout reform.
objection: Research and practical experience suggest that an election-day holiday by itself is not especially effective at increasing turnout compared with more direct voting-access reforms.

target: AG1's claim that cross-party support and OECD weekend/holiday practice show the policy is workable and appropriate.
objection: Public support and foreign precedent do not show that a U.S. federal holiday alone would remove the binding work-time barriers that matter for turnout, especially if private employers remain open.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday would leave low-income voters with persistent scheduling barriers because private employers need not close.
objection: In practice, a national holiday commonly leads schools, government offices, and many employers to operate on reduced or holiday schedules, so it can still reduce time conflicts for a substantial portion of voters even without a universal legal requirement.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday could widen inequities merely because not every employer must close.
objection: The fact that a holiday does not force all employers to close does not by itself show inequities would worsen; reducing the scheduling conflict for constrained voters is not inherently an inequity-worsening mechanism.

target: AG1's response that school closures and caregiving time make the holiday helpful even if some work conflicts persist.
objection: For low-income hourly workers whose main barrier is an assigned work shift, school or childcare flexibility does not solve the problem because freed caregiving time cannot be used to vote while the person is still required to be at work.

target: AG1's assumption that removing school/childcare constraints meaningfully helps low-income voters even when work conflicts remain.
objection: A federal holiday still leaves many low-income retail and service workers on scheduled shifts, so the work-time barrier remains for the group most constrained by time.

target: AG1's claim that increased civic motivation can raise participation even if some work-time conflicts remain.
objection: If voters cannot actually get time away from work, then higher civic motivation does not substitute for a missing opportunity to vote and therefore does not meaningfully increase participation among the most constrained voters.

target: AG1's reliance on the existence of weekend/holiday elections in many OECD countries as evidence that a holiday approach is effective.
objection: Those countries' results depend on broader labor protections and election-administration systems, so their weekend/holiday elections do not show that a U.S. holiday-only policy would remove the binding work-time constraints faced by low-income voters.

target: AG1's use of strong public support as evidence that the policy is warranted.
objection: Broad support does not answer whether the policy actually improves voting access for the most constrained workers or whether it leaves key barriers untouched because private employers can still schedule people to work.

target: AG1's claim that Election Day as a national holiday is justified because it reduces major obstacles for many voters even if not all barriers disappear.
objection: A policy is not well justified merely because it reduces some scheduling conflicts; if it does not reliably remove the binding work-time barrier for low-income hourly workers, it is an unreliable voting-access reform and may mainly benefit people with more flexibility.
